newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Pressure mounts on Mobutu to quit Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Mobutu to quit Zaire.

text.p: Military and diplomatic pressure mounted on Zaire's vetaran President Mobutu Sese Seko, now resting at a military camp in the capital Kinshasa, to allow a peaceful transfer to Laurent Kabila's rebels.
U.S. officials in Washington said it might be only one or two days before Kabila's forces took the city. "He'll be coming. There's no doubt about it," one official told Reuters.

An envoy from the United States, which backed Mobutu for three decades as a Cold War ally, said he was visiting Kabila's southern Lubumbashi headquarters to prepare a "soft landing" without bloodshed after the rebels entered Kinshasa.

Kabila said his forces were less than 60 km (35 miles) from Kinshasa's Ndjili international airport, which is 25 km (16 miles) from the city centre. He said he would guarantee Mobutu's safety if he handed over before the troops arrived.
"If Mobutu hands over power before we enter Kinshasa, I will guarantee his safety and that of his biological family. But if he does not, we will have to chase him away in humiliation," Kabila said.

He and Mobutu, who dominated the sprawling African country for more than 30 years, held ship-borne talks hosted by South Africa's President Nelson Mandela on Sunday but failed to agree terms for Mobutu's departure.
Some Zaire government officials said Mobutu, who returned to Kinshasa on Monday, made an immense concession at the 90-minute talks by even offering to hand over to an elected transition president.
Enfeebled by prostate cancer, Mobutu, 66, has seen his hold on the mineral-rich state at broken in little more than seven months by the Tutsi-dominated rebels.

He had ruled with cunning and guile since 1965, winning U.S. support as a bulwark against Soviet communist expansion. But after the Cold War, Washington lost its need for him and moved closer to Uganda and Rwanda, key backers of the rebels.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson met Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and Rwandan strongman Major-General Paul Kagame on Monday before going to Lubumbashi for talks with Kabila.
"President Museveni and General Kagame are key players on the scene here. We would like to make Kabila's entry as peaceful as possible. We want a soft landing followed by elections," Richardson said.
One-time Marxist Kabila's rebels now hold three quarters of Zaire and many local people have welcomed a change from corruption that pauperised them despite Zaire's mineral wealth.
In Kinshasa, people apparently fear a last stand by units of the Special Presidential Division, recruited from Mobutu's northern Ngbandi and related tribes, more than the coming of the rebels.

On the road down which the rebels are advancing, witnesses saw troops manning a bridge about 30 km (18 miles) from the capital. But Kinshasa was calm and there were no signs of increased military activity in the city centre.
Troops from the United States, former colonial power Belgium, France and Britain are ready in Congo, across the river from Kinshasa, to evacuate Western nationals if violence erupts.
